strengths: Strong theoretical contributions: Clean approximation-theoretic separations between rational and smooth-activation networks (O(log³log(1/ε)) vs Ω(log(1/ε))), rigorously proven with constructive proofs using classical approximation theory

Comprehensive and rigorous mathematical framework: Well-executed proofs extending from scalar to network level, gated activations, and transformers; sophisticated use of AGM-based methods and condenser capacity analysis

Addresses practical complications: Section 3.5 and Appendix D provide detailed analysis of rational-normalization incompatibility, including specific conditioning and variance amplification mechanisms—goes beyond typical theory-only papers

Excellent experimental rigor: Multiple domains (vision, RL, transformers), multiple seeds (5), controlled architectures, both with/without normalization tested, extensive hyperparameter documentation, code to be released
Honest treatment of limitations: Explicitly acknowledges experimental scale constraints (single GPU, no LLM-scale training) and theoretical-practical gaps rather than overstating claims
weaknesses: Critical theory-practice gap: Theory assumes compact domains with bounded parameters; practice uses unbounded inputs with normalization. Most damaging: Figure 2 shows learned rationals remain smooth in high-density regions despite theory motivating non-smooth approximation, contradicting the central premise that advantages come from approximating kinks/sharp transitions

Modest empirical improvements with significant overhead: CIFAR-10 gains ~1-2% (but 5-15% slower); offline RL wins 5/6 settings with small margins; Tiny ImageNet shows marginal improvements. Runtime overhead and normalization-induced drops often negate accuracy gains

Normalization incompatibility is a major unresolved practical blocker: Tables 2,5 show substantial performance drops with standard normalization layers (e.g., VGG4: 90.62→88.11 with GroupNorm). Proposed solution (removing normalization) works only for specific architectures and fails for others, severely limiting real-world applicability since normalization is ubiquitous in modern deep learning

Limited experimental scale and scope: Only small-to-mid scale models (max ~60M parameters); no LLM-scale validation despite mentioning it as motivation. Single-GPU experiments unclear if gains persist with distributed training and batch norm. At larger scales, normalization becomes more critical, potentially exacerbating rational-normalization problems

Theory doesn't explain empirical gains: The hard instances in lower bounds (rational functions with nearby poles) don't appear in learned representations. Theory provides worst-case analysis but is silent on average-case or typical learning problems. Why would flexible rationals provide consistent gains on smooth learning tasks like image classification?

Incomplete analysis of learned behavior: Figure 2 reveals that learned rationals become smooth—deserves deeper investigation but receives only a curious footnote. Limited analysis of what shapes are learned and why they don't exploit theoretical advantages; initialization sensitivity (Table 2: Rational 1 vs 2) suggests method may be brittle

Presentation could better connect theory to practice: 36 pages, dense development; intuition for key results (Theorem 3.1) should precede proofs. Why should practitioners care about approximating GELU to error ε? How does this translate to practical benefits? The gap isn't clearly bridged

Limited novelty in activation design: Uses existing Padé activations (Delfosse et al. 2020); 'safe' parameterization is a minor modification. Main contribution is theoretical justification rather than methodological innovation

strengths: Novel approximation-theoretic separations establishing exponential gap (O(log³log(1/ε)) vs Ω(log(1/ε))) between rational and smooth activations with rigorous constructive proofs
Comprehensive theoretical coverage: 15+ activation families, gated activations, and transformer architectures all rigorously analyzed
Rigorous experimental methodology with proper controls (identical architectures/optimizers), multiple seeds, statistical reporting, and experiments across vision and offline RL domains
Valuable formal analysis of normalization-rational activation interactions (Section 3.5, Appendix D) identifying non-identifiability and polynomial coefficient sensitivity issues
Excellent reproducibility practices: detailed hyperparameters, multi-seed evaluation, comprehensive appendices, code promised, all datasets public
Clear presentation with effective visualizations (learning curves, activation evolution snapshots) that provide interpretable insights into learned activations
weaknesses: Significant gap between theory and practice: theoretical results construct specific approximations to achieve log³log bounds, but practice uses adaptive gradient descent without guarantees these constructions are recovered; no analysis of optimization dynamics

Modest and inconsistent empirical improvements: CIFAR-10 gains ~1.5% (Table 2), Tiny ImageNet differences <0.5% (Table 5), offline RL improvements largest only in HalfCheetah (Table 3); largest gains occur only with non-standard normalization-free settings
Non-negligible computational overhead: 4 extra minutes for VGG (8% slowdown), 15-20 steps overhead in offline RL; undermines parameter-efficiency motivation
Limited experimental scale: largest models are ViT-Small and Swin-Tiny; no ImageNet or LLM-scale experiments; unclear if expressivity advantages matter at practical model sizes

Theoretical assumptions don't fully capture practice: hidden constants in complexity bounds unspecified; bounded parameters assumed during optimization; compact domain assumptions may not hold during training

Theory-practice gap on when advantages apply: Figure 2 reveals learned rationals remain smooth in regions where most activations occur, contradicting prediction that high-curvature structure provides benefits
Requires careful hyperparameter tuning: initialization targets and learning rate multipliers vary by architecture (0.5 to 8x, Tables 6 and 10); not a drop-in replacement for existing activations

strengths: Rigorous theoretical contributions with quantitative approximation-theoretic separations (Theorems 4.1-4.4) and constructive proofs using classical rational approximation theory
Comprehensive scope extending results to 15+ activation functions, full networks, gated activations, and transformer architectures

Sophisticated analysis of practical challenges: Section 4.5 and Appendix D rigorously formalize how normalization interacts negatively with adaptive rationals through non-identifiability and gradient noise amplification
Cross-domain empirical validation showing consistent improvements across vision (CIFAR-10, Tiny ImageNet) and offline RL with controlled experimental protocols
High technical quality with detailed proofs, careful error propagation analysis (Appendix C), and numerical verification of theoretical convergence rates (Figure 5)
Honest acknowledgment of limitations and practical challenges (theory-practice gap, scale constraints, need for safe Padé variant), enhancing credibility
weaknesses: Significant theory-practice gap: theoretical results apply to approximation on compact domains with uniform error bounds, but connection to generalization and stochastic training is not established; constants in O(·) and Ω(·) notation not made explicit
Limited practical improvements despite strong theory (1-2% on CIFAR-10, <1% on Tiny ImageNet) with inconsistent gains in offline RL, questioning practical significance of theoretical advantages

Experimental scale constraints severely limit confidence: all experiments on single RTX 4070 laptop, no LLM-scale evaluation, only 3 MuJoCo tasks, small vision models—acknowledging these limitations doesn't resolve the issue

Practical training requires workarounds diverging from theory: safe Padé variant with absolute value (Equation 18) replaces theoretical rational construction; normalization layers cause ~1% performance drop for rationals; best results require removing LayerNorm entirely

Incomplete experimental analysis: limited investigation of why rationals help, missing ablation studies, no systematic study of when benefits manifest, missing comparison with simply using wider networks at matched parameter budgets

Generalization bounds absent: lower bounds apply to worst-case rational functions not typical tasks; no sample complexity analysis or connection between approximation error and generalization error provided

Questionable fairness of comparisons: rational networks have additional trainable parameters (coefficients) beyond baseline 'fixed' activations; initialization-dependent results (Table 2); 'best over training' selection could introduce bias

Limited exploration of learnable activation alternatives (learnable Swish, polynomial activations) and architectural comparisons (width/depth modifications); no comparison with other learnable schemes
